P1.evidence: P1a not applicable — no setter and no notes. No frame of any kind was set: nothing about how the call would run, what would be covered or what the prospect should expect, and no agreement was sought. The call opened straight into qualification: "how long have you been following Trevor and how well do you know Kettlebells?" P1d partial — "So what brought you here?" and "is there anything in particular that you've been trying to fix for some time?" are in the right territory, but the second is framed as a problem question and drew a flat deflection ("No, I just want to build a bit more muscle") which was never worked past. The absence of a frame is the root of what goes wrong later: with no agreed structure, the prospect set the agenda, asked for price twelve minutes in, and got it.

P2.evidence: The strongest baseline in the batch on the checks that were run, and it is worth saying so: this is the only call in the batch where P2h and P2i were actually asked — "And in terms of your energy levels, sleep?" produced six to seven hours and post-lunch dips. P2b hit: "actually, what do you do for work? Is it, like, mostly in front of a computer, sitting all day?" P2e hit via "And before that, what did you do?" P2g hit and properly pursued — "walk me through, like, typical day of eating", then "do you go out very often?", then "Every second day?", which is what surfaced eating out almost daily. P2a partial: age 46 came out of a rep question about what got him to the gym, but height and weight were never asked despite a fat-loss goal. P2c miss — health conditions never asked. P2d is the consequential one, scored partial: he asked the question well ("How about injuries?"), received a disclosure of an acute back injury from the previous night, and then closed it down with a leading question that invited the answer he wanted — "But there's nothing serious that will disqualify you from working?" He did follow with limitations and stiffness questions, so the check was run, but the material disclosure was disposed of rather than explored. P2f miss.

P3.evidence: He ran the ladder and got nothing, then stopped. P3d is a genuine hit and he pushed harder than on most calls in this batch — "what's the big why? What's the big goal that you want to achieve?", then "What for? Why?", then "Why?" again. Three attempts. The answers stayed at the surface: "Just to be in good health and look good", "I just want to be in very good health for the longest time possible", "Because I want to have a good life." P3c hit and well phrased: "And what would that allow you to do that you cannot right now? Is there something that you're missing?", answered "No." Credit for asking. The failure is what came next — rather than changing angle he abandoned the phase entirely and moved to explaining the programme. P3f, P3g and P3h were never attempted, so nothing about work, ageing, mortality, relationships or identity was ever opened, and there was no reflect-back to test. With a 46-year-old who volunteered that he is starting to lose muscle and that his metabolism has changed, there was an obvious longevity thread available and it was not pulled.

P4.evidence: P4a hit — "And before that, what did you do?" — and that is the whole phase. He never asked what happened with the previous approaches, never asked why anything did or did not stick, and never asked what is actually getting in the way. The root cause was then handed to him unprompted and after the price: "The big question for me is the question of self-discipline, something I know I lack in certain areas." Under the scoring rule that is a miss on P4e, and it is also the single largest missed opportunity on the call — the prospect named the exact problem the accountability pillar exists to solve, and the rep responded with a generic "this is actually where Trevor comes in handy" rather than working it. He also never asked the one obvious question: the prospect is ending coaching that worked, so what specifically happens when it stops.

P5.evidence: Entirely absent. No cost of inaction was raised in any form — no two-year question, no settle test, no "why not", no line in the sand. This is the fifth sales call in the batch and the fifth with P5 scoring miss or partial, which now reads as a settled habit rather than a lapse. It is especially costly here because the prospect had supplied the raw material himself in the first three minutes: "at this age, I'm starting to lose muscle", the belly that has been growing, the metabolism that is not what it was. A two-year question against that would have cost nothing and would have given the later price objection something to be weighed against. Instead the only thing on the scale when $6,000 landed was $600.

P6.evidence: The clearest P6 failure in the batch. The script requires a genuine verbal yes before presenting anything; the prospect asked "Tell me about price. How does it work?" at 00:12:44 and the rep answered in the next breath — "the full transformation for the six months, it's 6K, $6,000" — with no belief question, no go-all-in question and no commitment of any kind first. The programme itself was then explained after the price rather than before it. There was a partial and unscripted gesture in this direction earlier, at 00:10:12, when the rep explained that Trevor needs people who will be fully committed, but it was framed as an explanation of the selection process and no commitment was actually requested. Nothing was in place to hold the price, and the prospect's answer forty seconds later — "Sounds like a lot to commit to" — went unaddressed.

P11.evidence: A price was given and declined; payment and onboarding were never reachable.

objection_plays.detail: The opening instinct was right and better than the batch average: "But is it more about the financial side or the commitment side from you?" is a real attempt to separate the objection, and it produced a truthful answer — "Both." From there almost nothing ran. He did not isolate with the scripted finances-aside question, did not use the SHOULD I versus HOW reframe, did not ask permission for an open financial conversation, and obtained none of the six financial-picture items. Most conspicuously, he never offered to break the payment up at all. This is the only call in the batch where affordability was named explicitly and no structure of any kind — no split, no instalments, no financing — was put on the table, in a week where the same rep offered an interest-free split to two other prospects, a $1,200 monthly plan to a third and Payva financing to a fourth. He made one value argument, the price-as-commitment-device line, which the prospect rebutted in six words, and then conceded.

A cheaper alternative that genuinely worked — the second of the two gaps already documented in the playbook, and a textbook instance of it. The prospect is three months into semi-private coaching he rates highly ("It's been very good"), is stopping it purely on cost, and is actively choosing between training at home and a gym membership: "I'm wondering whether I can now continue on my own." Nothing was asked about it. The rep never established what the coaching costs, never compared the two, never asked what the coach does that he could not do alone, and never positioned against a gym membership. All of that was available in the first ninety seconds of the call and none of it was used, which is why the $600 anchor arrived unopposed at the end.

Trigger present in substance — "I don't think I'm ready to commit for something like this" and "It's to think about a bit more." No moves ran. He did not ask whether the prospect believed the programme could get him to his goal, did not ask what was actually preventing him from getting started, did not use thinking-isn't-the-problem, and did not run the identity close. The call ended about seventy seconds after the objection landed.

Request for a smaller product. The prospect twice probed whether anything lighter exists — "He only offers that one program where it's just one-on-one with him?" and "maybe it's something that's not necessarily you need. And is it okay with two sessions a week, or is that not enough?" There is no scripted play for a prospect asking to buy less, and the rep simply confirmed the single offer. Worth logging as a script and product gap rather than a rep failure; see the signals file.
Prospect lives alone and no partner or consult requirement was raised.
No timing objection. He is available and actively deciding what to do next week.
No fear or doubt about the modality — he described the exercises as interesting and had no reservations about kettlebells.

notes: A call that got priced before it got sold. P5 and P6 were both absent and the $6,000 was given on request twelve minutes in, so it landed against nothing but the prospect's own $600 anchor. Credit where it is due: P2 was the most complete baseline in the batch, sleep and energy were actually asked about here and nowhere else, and the financial-versus-commitment diagnostic at the end was a good instinct. Three coaching points. First, when a prospect asks for price before the commitment check, defer it — that is the single decision that decided this call. Second, affordability was named and no payment structure was offered at all, which is inconsistent with how the same rep handled four other prospects the same week. Third, the whole call sits inside a known script gap — a man leaving coaching that worked, choosing between a gym and his living room — and not one question was asked about the alternative he is actually comparing against. Separately and outside the scoring: an acute back injury disclosed that morning was cleared with a leading question. See the flags file.
